Real Analysis — 02 · Topology of the Real Line and Continuity

Created2026-03-14|Updated2026-03-14|Mathematics > Real Analysis
|Post View:

Calculus states that a continuous function on a closed interval has a maximum and takes every value in between. Both facts can fail on an open interval or on the rationals, and the reason is not the function but the set it lives on. This post first studies subsets of R\mathbb{R}R — open, closed and compact sets — and then functions: the ε\varepsilonε–δ\deltaδ definition of a limit and of continuity, with fully worked δ\deltaδ's, the Extreme Value Theorem, the Intermediate Value Theorem, and uniform continuity. It builds directly on the Axiom of Completeness (Real Analysis 00) and on Bolzano–Weierstrass and sequences (Real Analysis 01).

Series map: 00 The Real Numbers & Completeness → 01 Sequences & Series → 02 Topology of ℝ & Continuity (this post) → 03 Differentiation & Taylor's Theorem → 04 The Riemann Integral → 05 Uniform Convergence & Power Series.

Learning Outcome

  • Define open sets, limit points, closed sets and closure, and decide which of these a given set is.
  • Define compactness by sequences and by open covers, and prove one direction of the Heine–Borel Theorem.
  • State the ε\varepsilonε–δ\deltaδ definition of a functional limit and its sequential criterion, and use the criterion to prove that a limit does not exist.
  • Prove continuity from the definition, with an explicit δ\deltaδ for f(x)=x2f(x) = x^2f(x)=x2 at a point, and check it numerically.
  • Prove that continuous images of compact sets are compact, and deduce the Extreme Value Theorem.
  • Prove the Intermediate Value Theorem using the supremum.
  • Define uniform continuity, show that 1/x1/x1/x and x2x^2x2 fail it on suitable domains, and prove that continuous functions on compact sets are uniformly continuous.
  • Describe the discontinuity sets of the Dirichlet and Thomae functions.

Chapter 1 — Open and closed sets

Terminology

  • ε\varepsilonε-neighbourhood — Vε(a)=(a−ε,a+ε)V_\varepsilon(a) = (a - \varepsilon, a + \varepsilon)Vε​(a)=(a−ε,a+ε).
  • Open set — O⊆RO \subseteq \mathbb{R}O⊆R is open if for every a∈Oa \in Oa∈O there is ε>0\varepsilon > 0ε>0 with Vε(a)⊆OV_\varepsilon(a) \subseteq OVε​(a)⊆O. Every point has some room around it inside the set.
  • Limit point of AAA — a point xxx (in AAA or not) such that every Vε(x)V_\varepsilon(x)Vε​(x) contains a point of AAA other than xxx.
  • Isolated point of AAA — a point of AAA that is not a limit point of AAA.
  • Closed set — a set that contains all of its limit points.
  • Closure — A‾=A∪L\overline{A} = A \cup LA=A∪L, where LLL is the set of limit points of AAA.
  • Complement — Ac=R∖AA^c = \mathbb{R} \setminus AAc=R∖A.

Examples of open sets

  • R\mathbb{R}R and ∅\emptyset∅ are open (the second vacuously).
  • Every open interval (a,b)(a, b)(a,b) is open: for x∈(a,b)x \in (a,b)x∈(a,b) take ε=min⁡(x−a, b−x)\varepsilon = \min(x - a,\ b - x)ε=min(x−a, b−x); then Vε(x)⊆(a,b)V_\varepsilon(x) \subseteq (a,b)Vε​(x)⊆(a,b).
  • [0,1)[0, 1)[0,1) is not open: no neighbourhood of 000 fits inside it.

Theorem. (i) Any union of open sets is open. (ii) A finite intersection of open sets is open.

Proof. (i) A point of the union lies in some OλO_\lambdaOλ​, and a neighbourhood inside OλO_\lambdaOλ​ is inside the union. (ii) If a∈O1∩⋯∩ONa \in O_1 \cap \cdots \cap O_Na∈O1​∩⋯∩ON​, choose εi\varepsilon_iεi​ with Vεi(a)⊆OiV_{\varepsilon_i}(a) \subseteq O_iVεi​​(a)⊆Oi​ and take ε=min⁡iεi>0\varepsilon = \min_i \varepsilon_i > 0ε=mini​εi​>0. ■\blacksquare■

The word "finite" in (ii) matters: ⋂n=1∞(−1n,1n)={0}\bigcap_{n=1}^\infty \left(-\frac1n, \frac1n\right) = \{0\}⋂n=1∞​(−n1​,n1​)={0}, which is not open. With infinitely many εi\varepsilon_iεi​ the minimum can be 000.

Limit points and closed sets

Theorem. xxx is a limit point of AAA if and only if x=lim⁡anx = \lim a_nx=liman​ for some sequence (an)(a_n)(an​) in AAA with an≠xa_n \ne xan​=x for all nnn.

Proof. (⇒\Rightarrow⇒) For each nnn pick an∈V1/n(x)∩Aa_n \in V_{1/n}(x) \cap Aan​∈V1/n​(x)∩A with an≠xa_n \ne xan​=x; then ∣an−x∣<1/n→0\lvert a_n - x \rvert < 1/n \to 0∣an​−x∣<1/n→0. (⇐\Leftarrow⇐) Given ε\varepsilonε, the terms ana_nan​ with nnn large lie in Vε(x)V_\varepsilon(x)Vε​(x), are in AAA, and differ from xxx. ■\blacksquare■

So a set is closed exactly when it contains the limit of every convergent sequence of its points (constant sequences included, for points of AAA itself).

Theorem. A set is open if and only if its complement is closed. Consequently, finite unions and arbitrary intersections of closed sets are closed (De Morgan's laws).

Proof of one direction. Let OOO be open and let xxx be a limit point of OcO^cOc. If x∈Ox \in Ox∈O, some Vε(x)⊆OV_\varepsilon(x) \subseteq OVε​(x)⊆O contains no point of OcO^cOc, contradicting that xxx is a limit point of OcO^cOc. So x∈Ocx \in O^cx∈Oc, and OcO^cOc is closed. ■\blacksquare■

The closure A‾\overline{A}A is the smallest closed set containing AAA; for example Q‾=R\overline{\mathbb{Q}} = \mathbb{R}Q​=R and (a,b)‾=[a,b]\overline{(a,b)} = [a,b](a,b)​=[a,b].

Watch out: "closed" is not the opposite of "open". A set can be both (R\mathbb{R}R, ∅\emptyset∅ — the only two such subsets of R\mathbb{R}R) or neither ([0,1)[0,1)[0,1), Q\mathbb{Q}Q).

Chapter 2 — Compact and connected sets

Terminology

  • Compact (sequential definition) — KKK is compact if every sequence in KKK has a subsequence that converges to a limit in KKK.
  • Open cover of AAA — a collection of open sets {Oλ}\{O_\lambda\}{Oλ​} whose union contains AAA. A finite subcover is a finite subcollection that still covers AAA.
  • Compact (cover definition) — every open cover of KKK has a finite subcover.
  • Bounded set — ∣x∣≤M\lvert x \rvert \le M∣x∣≤M for all xxx in the set, for some MMM.

Heine–Borel

Theorem (Heine–Borel). For K⊆RK \subseteq \mathbb{R}K⊆R the following are equivalent:
(i) KKK is compact (sequential definition);
(ii) KKK is closed and bounded;
(iii) every open cover of KKK has a finite subcover.

Proof of (ii) ⇒ (i). Let (xn)(x_n)(xn​) be a sequence in KKK. It is bounded because KKK is, so by Bolzano–Weierstrass (Real Analysis 01) it has a convergent subsequence xnk→xx_{n_k} \to xxnk​​→x. Either xxx equals infinitely many of the xnkx_{n_k}xnk​​, so x∈Kx \in Kx∈K, or it is a limit point of KKK, and then x∈Kx \in Kx∈K because KKK is closed. ■\blacksquare■

Proof of (i) ⇒ (ii). If KKK were unbounded, choose xn∈Kx_n \in Kxn​∈K with ∣xn∣>n\lvert x_n \rvert > n∣xn​∣>n; no subsequence is bounded, so none converges. If KKK were not closed, some limit point x∉Kx \notin Kx∈/K is the limit of a sequence in KKK; every subsequence also tends to x∉Kx \notin Kx∈/K. ■\blacksquare■

The equivalence with (iii) takes more work; see Abbott Section 3.3 and Rudin Theorems 2.40–2.41.

Nested compact sets. If K1⊇K2⊇K3⊇⋯K_1 \supseteq K_2 \supseteq K_3 \supseteq \cdotsK1​⊇K2​⊇K3​⊇⋯ are nonempty compact sets, then ⋂nKn≠∅\bigcap_n K_n \ne \emptyset⋂n​Kn​=∅. (Pick xn∈Knx_n \in K_nxn​∈Kn​. The sequence lies in K1K_1K1​, so a subsequence converges to some x∈K1x \in K_1x∈K1​. For each fixed mmm, the terms with nk≥mn_k \ge mnk​≥m lie in the closed set KmK_mKm​, so x∈Kmx \in K_mx∈Km​.) This generalizes the Nested Interval Property of Real Analysis 00 from intervals to any compact sets.

Examples. [0,1][0,1][0,1] and the Cantor set (an intersection of closed sets, inside [0,1][0,1][0,1]) are compact. (0,1)(0,1)(0,1) is not: the sequence 1/n1/n1/n has every subsequence tending to 0∉(0,1)0 \notin (0,1)0∈/(0,1). Equivalently, the open cover {(1/n,1):n≥2}\{(1/n, 1) : n \ge 2\}{(1/n,1):n≥2} of (0,1)(0,1)(0,1) has no finite subcover, since the union of finitely many of these sets is (1/N,1)(1/N, 1)(1/N,1) for the largest NNN used, which misses (0,1/N](0, 1/N](0,1/N]. R\mathbb{R}R is closed but not bounded, so not compact.

Trick: use the sequential definition when you have a sequence in hand (most proofs in this post). Use the cover definition to pass from "local" information at each point to a "global" statement with finitely many pieces.

Connected sets

Two nonempty sets A,BA, BA,B are separated if A‾∩B=∅\overline{A} \cap B = \emptysetA∩B=∅ and A∩B‾=∅A \cap \overline{B} = \emptysetA∩B=∅. A set is connected if it is not a union of two separated sets.

Theorem. A set E⊆RE \subseteq \mathbb{R}E⊆R is connected if and only if it is an interval: whenever a<c<ba < c < ba<c<b with a,b∈Ea, b \in Ea,b∈E, also c∈Ec \in Ec∈E.

Q\mathbb{Q}Q is not connected: Q={r<2}∪{r>2}\mathbb{Q} = \{r < \sqrt2\} \cup \{r > \sqrt2\}Q={r<2​}∪{r>2​} splits it into two separated pieces. This gap is exactly why the Intermediate Value Theorem fails for functions on Q\mathbb{Q}Q.

Chapter 3 — Limits of functions

Terminology

  • Functional limit — let f:A→Rf : A \to \mathbb{R}f:A→R and let ccc be a limit point of AAA. Then lim⁡x→cf(x)=L\lim_{x \to c} f(x) = Llimx→c​f(x)=L means: for every ε>0\varepsilon > 0ε>0 there is δ>0\delta > 0δ>0 such that for all x∈Ax \in Ax∈A with 0<∣x−c∣<δ0 < \lvert x - c \rvert < \delta0<∣x−c∣<δ, ∣f(x)−L∣<ε\lvert f(x) - L \rvert < \varepsilon∣f(x)−L∣<ε.
  • The condition 0<∣x−c∣0 < \lvert x - c \rvert0<∣x−c∣ means the value f(c)f(c)f(c) (if it exists) plays no role in the limit.

A first example

Claim. lim⁡x→2(3x+1)=7\lim_{x \to 2} (3x + 1) = 7limx→2​(3x+1)=7.

Proof. ∣(3x+1)−7∣=3∣x−2∣\lvert (3x + 1) - 7 \rvert = 3 \lvert x - 2 \rvert∣(3x+1)−7∣=3∣x−2∣. Given ε>0\varepsilon > 0ε>0, let δ=ε/3\delta = \varepsilon / 3δ=ε/3. If 0<∣x−2∣<δ0 < \lvert x - 2 \rvert < \delta0<∣x−2∣<δ then ∣(3x+1)−7∣<3δ=ε\lvert (3x+1) - 7 \rvert < 3\delta = \varepsilon∣(3x+1)−7∣<3δ=ε. ■\blacksquare■

For a linear function, δ\deltaδ is simply ε\varepsilonε divided by the slope. Nonlinear functions need one extra step (Chapter 4).

The sequential criterion

Theorem. lim⁡x→cf(x)=L\lim_{x \to c} f(x) = Llimx→c​f(x)=L if and only if for every sequence (xn)(x_n)(xn​) in AAA with xn≠cx_n \ne cxn​=c and xn→cx_n \to cxn​→c, the sequence f(xn)→Lf(x_n) \to Lf(xn​)→L.

Proof of (⇒). Let ε>0\varepsilon > 0ε>0 and take the δ\deltaδ from the definition. Since xn→cx_n \to cxn​→c, there is NNN with ∣xn−c∣<δ\lvert x_n - c \rvert < \delta∣xn​−c∣<δ for n≥Nn \ge Nn≥N, and xn≠cx_n \ne cxn​=c. So ∣f(xn)−L∣<ε\lvert f(x_n) - L \rvert < \varepsilon∣f(xn​)−L∣<ε for n≥Nn \ge Nn≥N. ■\blacksquare■

Proof of (⇐). Suppose the limit is not LLL. Negating the definition (Real Analysis 00): there is ε0>0\varepsilon_0 > 0ε0​>0 such that for every δ>0\delta > 0δ>0 some x∈Ax \in Ax∈A has 0<∣x−c∣<δ0 < \lvert x - c \rvert < \delta0<∣x−c∣<δ and ∣f(x)−L∣≥ε0\lvert f(x) - L \rvert \ge \varepsilon_0∣f(x)−L∣≥ε0​. Apply this with δ=1/n\delta = 1/nδ=1/n for each nnn to get xn≠cx_n \ne cxn​=c with ∣xn−c∣<1/n\lvert x_n - c \rvert < 1/n∣xn​−c∣<1/n, so xn→cx_n \to cxn​→c, but ∣f(xn)−L∣≥ε0\lvert f(x_n) - L \rvert \ge \varepsilon_0∣f(xn​)−L∣≥ε0​ for all nnn, so f(xn)↛Lf(x_n) \not\to Lf(xn​)→L. ■\blacksquare■

The same pattern — negate the ε\varepsilonε–δ\deltaδ statement, then use δ=1/n\delta = 1/nδ=1/n to build a sequence — proves the sequential criteria for continuity and for uniform continuity below.

Corollary (divergence criterion). If two sequences xn→cx_n \to cxn​→c and yn→cy_n \to cyn​→c (terms ≠c\ne c=c) have f(xn)f(x_n)f(xn​) and f(yn)f(y_n)f(yn​) tending to different limits, then lim⁡x→cf(x)\lim_{x \to c} f(x)limx→c​f(x) does not exist.

Example. f(x)=sin⁡(1/x)f(x) = \sin(1/x)f(x)=sin(1/x) at c=0c = 0c=0. Take xn=12nπx_n = \frac{1}{2n\pi}xn​=2nπ1​ and yn=12nπ+π/2y_n = \frac{1}{2n\pi + \pi/2}yn​=2nπ+π/21​. Both tend to 000, but sin⁡(1/xn)=sin⁡(2nπ)=0\sin(1/x_n) = \sin(2n\pi) = 0sin(1/xn​)=sin(2nπ)=0 and sin⁡(1/yn)=sin⁡(2nπ+π/2)=1\sin(1/y_n) = \sin(2n\pi + \pi/2) = 1sin(1/yn​)=sin(2nπ+π/2)=1 for every nnn. The limit does not exist: the graph oscillates between −1-1−1 and 111 infinitely often near 000.

Chapter 4 — Continuity

Terminology

  • Removable discontinuity at ccc — lim⁡x→cf(x)\lim_{x \to c} f(x)limx→c​f(x) exists but differs from f(c)f(c)f(c) (or f(c)f(c)f(c) is undefined).
  • Jump discontinuity — the one-sided limits lim⁡x→c−f(x)\lim_{x \to c^-} f(x)limx→c−​f(x) and lim⁡x→c+f(x)\lim_{x \to c^+} f(x)limx→c+​f(x) both exist but are different.
  • Essential discontinuity — at least one one-sided limit does not exist, as for sin⁡(1/x)\sin(1/x)sin(1/x) at 000.
  • Lipschitz function — there is K≥0K \ge 0K≥0 with ∣f(x)−f(y)∣≤K∣x−y∣\lvert f(x) - f(y) \rvert \le K \lvert x - y \rvert∣f(x)−f(y)∣≤K∣x−y∣ for all x,yx, yx,y in the domain.

Definition

f:A→Rf : A \to \mathbb{R}f:A→R is continuous at c∈Ac \in Ac∈A if for every ε>0\varepsilon > 0ε>0 there is δ>0\delta > 0δ>0 such that for all x∈Ax \in Ax∈A with ∣x−c∣<δ\lvert x - c \rvert < \delta∣x−c∣<δ, ∣f(x)−f(c)∣<ε\lvert f(x) - f(c) \rvert < \varepsilon∣f(x)−f(c)∣<ε. It is continuous on AAA if it is continuous at every point of AAA.

Equivalently (sequential criterion): fff is continuous at ccc if and only if xn→cx_n \to cxn​→c with xn∈Ax_n \in Axn​∈A implies f(xn)→f(c)f(x_n) \to f(c)f(xn​)→f(c). If ccc is a limit point of AAA, this is the same as lim⁡x→cf(x)=f(c)\lim_{x \to c} f(x) = f(c)limx→c​f(x)=f(c). At an isolated point of AAA every function is continuous.

Worked example: a delta for x squared at c = 3

Claim. f(x)=x2f(x) = x^2f(x)=x2 is continuous at c=3c = 3c=3.

Scratch work. Factor: ∣x2−9∣=∣x−3∣ ∣x+3∣\lvert x^2 - 9 \rvert = \lvert x - 3 \rvert \, \lvert x + 3 \rvert∣x2−9∣=∣x−3∣∣x+3∣. ∣x2−9∣<7∣x−3∣.\lvert x^2 - 9 \rvert < 7 \lvert x - 3 \rvert. ∣x2−9∣<7∣x−3∣.

Trick: the "δ=min⁡(1,… )\delta = \min(1, \dots)δ=min(1,…)" move is the standard way to handle a nonlinear factor: first restrict xxx to a fixed interval around ccc to bound the awkward factor by a constant, then divide ε\varepsilonε by that constant.

Building continuous functions

Algebraic Continuity Theorem. If fff and ggg are continuous at ccc, so are kfkfkf, f+gf + gf+g, fgfgfg, and f/gf/gf/g (if g(c)≠0g(c) \ne 0g(c)=0).

Proof. Use the sequential criterion: if xn→cx_n \to cxn​→c then f(xn)→f(c)f(x_n) \to f(c)f(xn​)→f(c) and g(xn)→g(c)g(x_n) \to g(c)g(xn​)→g(c), and the Algebraic Limit Theorem (Real Analysis 01) does the rest. ■\blacksquare■

Since f(x)=xf(x) = xf(x)=x and constants are continuous, every polynomial is continuous on R\mathbb{R}R, and every rational function is continuous wherever its denominator is not zero.

Composition. If ggg is continuous at ccc and fff is continuous at g(c)g(c)g(c), then f∘gf \circ gf∘g is continuous at ccc.

Proof. Let ε>0\varepsilon > 0ε>0. Choose η>0\eta > 0η>0 with ∣y−g(c)∣<η⇒∣f(y)−f(g(c))∣<ε\lvert y - g(c) \rvert < \eta \Rightarrow \lvert f(y) - f(g(c)) \rvert < \varepsilon∣y−g(c)∣<η⇒∣f(y)−f(g(c))∣<ε. Then choose δ>0\delta > 0δ>0 with ∣x−c∣<δ⇒∣g(x)−g(c)∣<η\lvert x - c \rvert < \delta \Rightarrow \lvert g(x) - g(c) \rvert < \eta∣x−c∣<δ⇒∣g(x)−g(c)∣<η. Chaining, ∣x−c∣<δ⇒∣f(g(x))−f(g(c))∣<ε\lvert x - c \rvert < \delta \Rightarrow \lvert f(g(x)) - f(g(c)) \rvert < \varepsilon∣x−c∣<δ⇒∣f(g(x))−f(g(c))∣<ε. ■\blacksquare■

So 1+x2\sqrt{1 + x^2}1+x2​, sin⁡(x3)\sin(x^3)sin(x3) and ecos⁡xe^{\cos x}ecosx are continuous (given that the square root, sine, cosine and exponential functions are continuous on their domains).

Chapter 5 — Continuous functions on compact sets and intervals

Compactness is preserved

Theorem. If f:K→Rf : K \to \mathbb{R}f:K→R is continuous and KKK is compact, then f(K)={f(x):x∈K}f(K) = \{f(x) : x \in K\}f(K)={f(x):x∈K} is compact.

Proof. Let (yn)(y_n)(yn​) be a sequence in f(K)f(K)f(K); write yn=f(xn)y_n = f(x_n)yn​=f(xn​) with xn∈Kx_n \in Kxn​∈K. By compactness a subsequence xnk→x∈Kx_{n_k} \to x \in Kxnk​​→x∈K. Compact domains fix everything

Theorem. A continuous function on a compact set KKK is uniformly continuous on KKK.

Proof. Suppose not. By the sequential criterion there are ε0>0\varepsilon_0 > 0ε0​>0 and xn,yn∈Kx_n, y_n \in Kxn​,yn​∈K with ∣xn−yn∣→0\lvert x_n - y_n \rvert \to 0∣xn​−yn​∣→0 and ∣f(xn)−f(yn)∣≥ε0\lvert f(x_n) - f(y_n) \rvert \ge \varepsilon_0∣f(xn​)−f(yn​)∣≥ε0​. By compactness a subsequence xnk→x∈Kx_{n_k} \to x \in Kxnk​​→x∈K. Then

∣ynk−x∣≤∣ynk−xnk∣+∣xnk−x∣→0,\lvert y_{n_k} - x \rvert \le \lvert y_{n_k} - x_{n_k} \rvert + \lvert x_{n_k} - x \rvert \to 0, ∣ynk​​−x∣≤∣ynk​​−xnk​​∣+∣xnk​​−x∣→0,

so ynk→xy_{n_k} \to xynk​​→x too. By continuity at xxx, both f(xnk)f(x_{n_k})f(xnk​​) and f(ynk)f(y_{n_k})f(ynk​​) tend to f(x)f(x)f(x), so ∣f(xnk)−f(ynk)∣→0\lvert f(x_{n_k}) - f(y_{n_k}) \rvert \to 0∣f(xnk​​)−f(ynk​​)∣→0. This contradicts ∣f(xnk)−f(ynk)∣≥ε0\lvert f(x_{n_k}) - f(y_{n_k}) \rvert \ge \varepsilon_0∣f(xnk​​)−f(ynk​​)∣≥ε0​. ■\blacksquare■

This theorem is the reason the Riemann integral of a continuous function on [a,b][a, b][a,b] exists (Real Analysis 04): one δ\deltaδ for the whole interval controls every subinterval of a partition at once.

Watch out: "continuous on (0,1)(0,1)(0,1) and bounded" does not give uniform continuity (sin⁡(1/x)\sin(1/x)sin(1/x)), and neither does "continuous on a closed set" (x2x^2x2 on R\mathbb{R}R). The hypothesis is closed and bounded.

Practice Exercises

1. Is A={1+1/n:n∈N}∪{1}A = \{1 + 1/n : n \in \mathbb{N}\} \cup \{1\}A={1+1/n:n∈N}∪{1} open, closed, compact? Find its limit points.

Solution

The only limit point is 111, which is in AAA, so AAA is closed. It is bounded (inside [1,2][1, 2][1,2]), so it is compact by Heine–Borel. It is not open: no neighbourhood of 222 lies in AAA.

2. Show directly from the cover definition that [0,∞)[0, \infty)[0,∞) is not compact.

What's next

Real Analysis 03 defines the derivative as a functional limit and proves the theorems that make calculus work, such as the Mean Value Theorem (whose proof needs the Extreme Value Theorem from this post) and Taylor's theorem with remainder.

References

  • Stephen Abbott, Understanding Analysis, 2nd edition, Springer, 2015 — Chapter 3 (basic topology of R\mathbb{R}R) and Chapter 4 (functional limits and continuity; Section 4.6 on sets of discontinuity).
  • Walter Rudin, Principles of Mathematical Analysis, 3rd edition, McGraw-Hill, 1976 — Chapter 2 (basic topology) and Chapter 4 (continuity).
  • Robert G. Bartle and Donald R. Sherbert, Introduction to Real Analysis, 4th edition, Wiley, 2011 — Chapters 4–5 and 11.
  • Terence Tao, Analysis I, 4th edition, Springer, 2022 — Chapter 9 (continuous functions on R\mathbb{R}R).
  • Michael Spivak, Calculus, 4th edition, Publish or Perish, 2008 — Chapters 5–8 (limits, continuity, the three hard theorems).
  • MIT OpenCourseWare, 18.100A Real Analysis, Fall 2020 (Casey Rodriguez), lecture notes: https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-100a-real-analysis-fall-2020/
